c.tagline: An adobe desert oasis town ringed by geysers, salt flats, and the otherworldly Valle de la Luna
langs: Kunza (nearly extinct Atacameño language, largely ceremonial)

card: Widely accepted at hotels and tour agencies; cash useful for small shops

taxi.fareNote: Most sightseeing (Valle de la Luna, El Tatio geysers, salt flats) is done via organized tour rather than taxi

emergency.note: 133 for police, 131 for medical emergencies; response times can be slower given the town's remoteness

religion: Indigenous Atacameño spiritual traditions (practiced alongside Christianity by some)
walk: San Pedro's small adobe town center is walkable; nearly all major attractions (Valle de la Luna, geysers, salt flats) require an organized tour or rental vehicle

safety.safety: Very safe town, though the surrounding desert and high-altitude sites demand preparation for sun, cold nights, and altitude
safety.crime: Very low crime; the main risks are altitude sickness and extreme desert temperature swings

hood_landmark.San Pedro Town Center: San Pedro's adobe church and central plaza
hood_landmark.Valle de la Luna (day-trip): The moon-like eroded salt formations of Valle de la Luna
hood_landmark.El Tatio Geysers (day-trip): El Tatio's steaming high-altitude geyser field
hood_landmark.Salar de Atacama (day-trip): The Salar de Atacama's flamingo-filled salt lagoons
hood_landmark.Laguna Cejar / Altiplanic Lagoons (day-t: Laguna Cejar's dense, buoyant swimming waters

avoid.reason: Unlit dirt streets at night and occasional theft from hostels and parked bikes — keep valuables secured.

hood_desc: The compact adobe town with most hotels, restaurants, and tour agencies; the practical base for the entire Atacama region.
A surreal lunar-like desert landscape a short drive from town, best visited at sunset when the colors intensify.
One of the world's highest-altitude geyser fields, best visited near sunrise when the steam plumes are most dramatic against the cold air.
A vast salt flat south of town, home to flamingo colonies and some of the clearest reflections in the Atacama.
A cluster of salt lagoons near San Pedro so dense with minerals that swimmers float effortlessly, popular for a late-afternoon dip.

water.note: Local tap water is high in minerals including arsenic; drink bottled or filtered.

transit.sys: Tour agency shuttles and local taxis; no formal public bus network within the desert sites
transit.hours: Tours often depart pre-dawn (for geysers) or late afternoon (for sunset sites)
transit.pay: Tours booked and paid through agencies in town
transit.map: Not centrally published; dozens of tour agencies line San Pedro's main street
transit.note: Renting a 4x4 is possible for independent travel, but most visitors join organized tours given the remoteness and altitude

transport.air: El Loa Airport (CJC) in Calama, about 1.5 hr away, with domestic flights from Santiago
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect to Calama and onward to Santiago (about 20+ hr) or into Bolivia and Argentina
transport.car: Rental cars (ideally 4x4) available in Calama; many sites also require high-altitude driving experience

airport.name: El Loa Airport, Calama
airport.distance: ~100 km (1.5 hr) from San Pedro de Atacama
airport.transport: Shuttle bus or pre-arranged transfer from Calama

net.m: Moderate 4G coverage in town, minimal at remote desert sites
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels
net.ap: An Entel or Movistar Chile tourist SIM or eSIM

food.name: Lomo de llama
food.desc: Lean, dark, faintly gamey llama loin from the altiplano, usually grilled and plated with quinoa and Andean vegetable sauces.

places.name: Ckunna
places.note: Set in the town first schoolhouse; altiplano cooking with llama as the signature plate.

places.name: Adobe
places.note: Long-established courtyard restaurant with an open fire, a classic for grilled llama.

places.name: Baltinache
places.note: Small kitchen praised for careful cooking of local meats and Andean sides.

food.name: Quinoa dishes
food.desc: The Andean grain turns up in everything here, from quinoa risotto and stuffed peppers to quinoa sushi and quinoa-crusted fish.

places.name: Lola
places.note: Two kitchens in one, local and vegetarian, with well-rated quinoa and salmon plates.

places.name: Paacha
places.note: Bolivian-leaning menu doing quinoa sushi and corn-and-quinoa ceviche.

places.name: Todo Natural
places.note: Casual healthy cafe with quinoa bowls and salads, handy before desert tours.

food.name: Empanadas atacamenas
food.desc: Baked or fried turnovers filled with beef pino, cheese or llama, sold from bakery windows and market stalls at all hours.

places.name: Feria Artesanal y mercado municipal
places.note: Market stalls with cheap fresh-baked empanadas, the local everyday version.

places.name: Las Delicias de Carmen
places.note: Family bakery-restaurant known for home-style empanadas and breakfasts.

places.name: La Casona
places.note: One of the oldest restaurants in town, reliable for empanadas and Chilean staples.

food.name: Calapurca
food.desc: Ancient Andean stew of llama or lamb, hominy corn and potatoes traditionally brought to the boil with a hot volcanic stone dropped into the pot.

places.name: Ckunna
places.note: Puts traditional Atacameno recipes on the menu, including altiplano stews.

places.name: Las Delicias de Carmen
places.note: Home cooking with rotating Andean soups and stews on the daily menu.

places.name: Feria Artesanal y mercado municipal
places.note: Market fondas ladle out cazuelas and hominy stews at lunchtime prices.

food.name: Sopaipillas con pebre
food.desc: Golden fried pumpkin-dough discs eaten hot with pebre salsa or drizzled with chancaca syrup, Chile favourite street snack.

places.name: Feria Artesanal y mercado municipal
places.note: Fried to order at the market snack counters, best in the cold desert evenings.

places.name: Las Delicias de Carmen
places.note: Serves them alongside soups as part of the home-style Chilean menu.

places.name: Caracoles street food stands
places.note: Evening carts along the main strip sell sopaipillas and completos.

food.name: Helados de rica-rica y chanar
food.desc: Artisan ice cream flavoured with desert botanicals: resinous rica-rica herb, sweet chanar pods, algarrobo and quinoa.

places.name: Babalu Heladeria
places.note: The town best-known ice cream shop, built around native desert flavours.

places.name: Todo Natural
places.note: Also does juices and desserts using local herbs and fruits.

food.name: Rica-rica sour
food.desc: Pisco sour infused with rica-rica, the aromatic altiplano shrub, giving the classic Chilean cocktail a resinous desert edge.

places.name: Ckunna
places.note: Courtyard bar mixing pisco sours with native herbs before dinner.

places.name: Adobe
places.note: Fire-pit bar that is the town evening gathering place for sours.

places.name: Lola
places.note: Relaxed cafe-bar with rica-rica and standard pisco sours.

food.name: Mate de coca
food.desc: Coca leaf infusion drunk across the altiplano to ease the 2,400m altitude, poured free in most hotels and cafes.

places.name: Todo Natural
places.note: Herbal teas including coca and rica-rica infusions, good for acclimatising.

places.name: Feria Artesanal y mercado municipal
places.note: Stalls sell loose coca leaf and herbal blends to brew yourself.

places.name: Cafe Tierra
places.note: Popular breakfast cafe pouring coca and mountain-herb teas with fresh bread.

landmarks: Valle de la Luna (Moon Valley)
Wind-sculpted dunes, salt-crusted ridges and amphitheatres of rock blaze orange at sunset in the Atacama's most otherworldly landscape.
El Tatio Geysers
At dawn, over eighty geysers steam against the freezing Andean sky on one of the world's highest geothermal fields at 4,320 metres.
Lagunas Miscanti y Miñiques
Twin sapphire lakes cupped beneath snow-dusted volcanoes at 4,100 metres, where vicuñas graze the golden altiplano grasslands.
Laguna Chaxa (Salar de Atacama)
Three flamingo species feed in mirror-still brine pools amid the crackled crust of Chile's largest salt flat.
Iglesia de San Pedro de Atacama
A luminous whitewashed adobe church from the 17th century, roofed with cactus wood and leather, anchoring the oasis town's plaza.
Pukará de Quitor
A 12th-century pre-Inca hillside fortress of stone terraces overlooking the San Pedro River valley, with panoramic desert views from its summit.
Piedras Rojas & Salar de Aguas Calientes
Rust-red volcanic boulders meet a turquoise salt lagoon in one of the altiplano's most photographed, high-altitude colour spectacles.
Valle del Arcoíris (Rainbow Valley)
Mineral-streaked hills in greens, reds and creams ripple through this quiet valley, complemented by ancient Yerbas Buenas petroglyphs nearby.
Lagunas Escondidas de Baltinache
Seven hidden turquoise brine pools strung across blinding-white salt crust, where floaters bob effortlessly in hypersaline water.
Aldea de Tulor
The excavated circular adobe dwellings of a 2,800-year-old village, among Chile's oldest settlements, emerge hauntingly from the desert sand.

train.note: No passenger railway serves San Pedro - the Antofagasta-Bolivia line through the region carries freight only, and Chile's sole international passenger train is the Arica-Tacna service far to the north. Arrive by coach, or fly into Calama and take the hour-long transfer.

intl.to: Uyuni & La Paz (Bolivia) - via the Hito Cajón border
intl.op: Cruz del Norte / Trans Salvador — tickets through San Pedro agencies

intl.to: Salta & Jujuy (Argentina) - over the Paso de Jama, ~11 hr

bus.note: San Pedro sits at 2,400 m near two high Andean borders. The Bolivia route is usually sold as a three-day 4x4 salt-flats tour ending in Uyuni rather than a bus, crossing at Hito Cajón; the Argentina coaches climb the 4,200 m Paso de Jama and can be stopped by snow. Carry your passport and cash for border fees. Domestic buses to Calama take about 90 minutes on Turbus (https://www.turbus.cl/) and Frontera.

ferry.note: San Pedro de Atacama sits in the driest desert on earth, so there are no ferries of any kind.

half.name: Toconao
half.blurb: A small village of volcanic-stone architecture and a bell tower, sitting at the edge of the Salar de Atacama salt flat.

half.name: Termas de Puritama
half.blurb: A series of thermal pools fed by hot springs, set in a canyon with cacti-lined walls in the Andean foothills.

half.name: Calama and Chuquicamata
half.blurb: The nearest city serves as gateway to Chuquicamata, one of the world's largest open-pit copper mines, viewable on guided tours.
